r: EVT 1051 introduces the basic concepts of becoming a professional wedding planner and the fundamentals of managing an independent wedding-planning business: vendor coordination, budgeting, timelines, and client-facing administration. These tasks map to O*NET planning, scheduling, and external-communication activities, categories where observed-usage data already shows meaningful uptake for drafting proposals, budgets, and vendor correspondence. The course carries no licensure or accreditation lock, and as a lower-level survey it is not prerequisite scaffolding for other coursework, so neither institutional lock-in nor foundational role holds the rating down. Some protection comes from the live, real-time coordination inherent to executing an actual wedding day, which keeps the work from being purely digital. At 24 months, adoption among small independent wedding-planning businesses remains uneven, so the instrumental case is only partially eroded: Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft full wedding-planning packages — vendor shortlists, budgets, day-of timelines, contracts, client communications — competently and cheaply, consistent with productivity research showing large gains on professional writing and planning tasks. The description's emphasis on planning details and business administration, rather than embodied service delivery, means most of what this course teaches is executable by a capable model with light human direction. No accreditation or foundational-scaffolding factor caps the erosion, since the course neither gates licensure nor underlies later required coursework in this catalog. The live, in-person coordination of the wedding day itself is a genuine residue, but it is a smaller share of the course's content than the planning and business-management material. The instrumental case for taking the course to acquire this specific knowledge is substantially eroded: High, with real uncertainty about how much day-of coordination still requires a hired human planner.

A decade out, the central case has AI-assisted planning tools routinely handling vendor sourcing, budgeting, contract drafting, and client communication for weddings, consistent with task-exposure research's classification of planning-heavy administrative work as highly exposed. Nothing in this course's description ties it to licensure, professional accreditation, or a required sequence, so no institutional or foundational cap holds the rating down at the ten-year horizon. The wide uncertainty band applies to how much of the live, in-person wedding-day role persists as paid human work versus AI-coordinated logistics with minimal on-site staffing — a genuinely open question this rating cannot resolve confidently. What is clearer is that the specific business-planning knowledge this introductory course conveys sits squarely inside AI's likely competence by 2036. The rating holds at High, hedged by real uncertainty about the embodied, client-facing residue of the wedding-planner role.
EVT 1051.d: This course introduces students to the basic concepts involved in becoming a professional wedding planner. It covers the various details of planning the wedding and the basics of managing an independent wedding planning business.

r: This survey course covers the segments of the events industry — meetings, expositions, events, conventions — the roles of destination marketing and management organizations, general-versus-service contractor relationships, and the planner's responsibilities for planning, organizing, directing, and controlling events. The content is largely informational and analytical, mapping to O*NET information-gathering and planning activities that observed-usage data shows are already common AI use cases for industry overviews and role summaries. There is no licensure or accreditation lock on this course, but it is structurally foundational: EVT 3000, EVT 3200, and EVT 4020 all list it as a prerequisite, making it substrate for three later required courses. At 24 months that scaffolding role, not task protection, is what keeps the rating from rising above Medium.

By 2031, AI systems will fluently explain industry structure, DMO and DMC functions, and contractor relationships, and could generate much of the descriptive and evaluative content this course currently teaches through instruction. Task-exposure research places this kind of explanatory, non-adversarial informational work well inside AI's competence, and diffusion of such tools into hospitality education is plausible on this horizon. Because the course is prerequisite substrate for three upper-division courses rather than a terminal course, the foundational-scaffolding cap that applied at 24 months no longer binds numerically at this horizon under the deterministic rule, and the base rate computed from rising task automatability governs instead. The instrumental case for a student to personally learn this material, rather than query a model for it on demand, erodes substantially: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI serving as an authoritative, interactive explainer of event-industry structure and stakeholder relationships, and the pure information-transmission function of this course is largely superseded by that capability. No accreditation or licensure requirement in hospitality holds the course in place the way a clinical or engineering mandate would elsewhere in the catalog, so the erosion is not capped by institutional lock-in at this horizon. The genuine uncertainty concerns how introductory industry-overview courses are taught and assessed once students can query capable models directly for the same content, and whether the prerequisite role for EVT 3000, 3200, and 4020 is preserved by restructuring the course around applied judgment rather than recall. The rating holds at High, reflecting that the descriptive core of the course is squarely within AI's likely long-run competence.
EVT 2010.d: This course presents an overview of the major segments of events industry: meetings, expositions, events, and conventions. The roles and responsibilities of destination marketing organizations and destination management companies will be reviewed. The relationship between general and service contractors and professional events will be examined and their specific functions will be discussed and evaluated. This course highlights the role of the event planner, whose responsibilities include planning, organizing, directing, and controlling various types of events.

r: The course teaches project management as applied to events: the project triangle, scope definition, work breakdown structures, task and precedence diagramming for scheduling, communications planning, and close-out with lessons learned. These are highly systematized, document-driven activities — O*NET planning, scheduling, and recording tasks — that already sit close to what generative tools produce competently, echoing productivity research on large speedups for structured planning and documentation work. The course carries no accreditation lock, and while it is a prerequisite for EVT 4100, that single downstream dependency is only moderately protective under the deterministic rule and does not trigger a cap. At 24 months, near-term diffusion into hospitality curricula and the still-developing student skill in structuring a WBS, precedence diagram, and schedule keep the applied-task erosion from being complete, though drafting assistance already touches parts of the workflow: Medium.

By 2031, AI project-planning tools will plausibly generate work breakdown structures, precedence diagrams, communications plans, and close-out reports for a described event with minimal human input, consistent with evidence on large productivity gains for structured planning and documentation tasks and on faster task completion when a capable assistant handles the drafting layer. The applied tasks this course teaches — building the schedule, the master task list, the stakeholder communications plan, the lessons-learned close-out — are concrete, template-like deliverables well inside that capability band. The single-course prerequisite link to EVT 4100 offers only moderate protection under the deterministic rule and does not cap the erosion at this horizon. The instrumental case for a student to personally construct these planning artifacts, rather than direct and check an AI-generated version, is substantially weakened: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing complete event project plans — scope, WBS, schedule, communications plan, close-out documentation — competently and quickly, and the manual-construction rationale for this course is largely eroded. No institutional or foundational factor holds the rating down at this horizon: there is no accreditation mandate in hospitality, and the course's one prerequisite relationship to EVT 4100 does not meet the threshold for a long-horizon cap. The genuine uncertainty is whether project-planning instruction shifts toward specifying requirements and verifying AI-generated plans rather than building them from scratch, a plausible pedagogical adaptation this rating cannot predict with confidence. The rating holds at High, reflecting that the concrete planning deliverables at the center of the course are squarely within AI's likely long-run competence.
EVT 2020.d: This course provides an overview of project management as an identification and explanation for the building blocks of an event from start to finish. The project triangle is introduced and demonstrates the construction of an event. Students will define the scope, create well-defined requirements, and develop work breakdown structures for an event. Task and precedence diagramming will be taught to develop the event schedule and master task list. Students will also learn to construct an event project communications plan for the purpose of communicating with internal and external stakeholders. The final portion of the course is designed to teach students to close out the function and visualize the lessons learned from the production of the event.

r: Students in this course interpret attendee food-and-beverage consumption patterns, identify service requirements and meal styles, distinguish on- from off-site catering requirements, examine catering-department relationships within a hotel, design sample group menus, and set pricing and contractual terms for group functions. This is predominantly analytical and planning work — O*NET estimating and coordinating activities applied to menu design and pricing — rather than hands-on food service, which keeps it closer to the exposed business-planning band than to embodied culinary execution. The course has no accreditation lock and is a corequisite feeding EVT 4100 rather than a heavily-relied-upon prerequisite, so foundational role does not meaningfully protect it. At 24 months, near-term diffusion limits and the course's applied-strategy framing keep the erosion only partial: Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft sample group menus, model attendee consumption patterns, generate pricing strategies, and structure catering contract terms with considerable fluency, consistent with evidence on strong productivity gains for structured business-writing and planning tasks. Because the course's applied work is described in analytical and strategic terms — interpreting consumption patterns, planning menus, determining pricing and contractual requirements — rather than physical food preparation or table service, the embodiment factor offers only moderate protection at best. No accreditation requirement binds catering-strategy instruction in this hospitality program, and the corequisite link to EVT 4100 does not meet the threshold for a long-horizon cap. The instrumental case for personally performing this strategic analysis, versus directing and checking an AI-generated version, is substantially eroded: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems competently generating catering strategy documents — menu proposals, pricing models, consumption-pattern analyses, contractual terms — for a described event or venue, and the strategic-planning rationale for this course is largely superseded. No institutional lock-in applies in this hospitality program, so the erosion is not capped by accreditation or licensure at this horizon. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much on-site catering-department coordination and real-time service-style judgment remain distinctly human as the analytical layer automates, a residue this course description does not emphasize strongly enough relative to its planning content to warrant additional protection. The rating holds at High, reflecting that the specific catering-strategy content taught here sits well inside AI's likely long-run planning and analytical competence.
EVT 3000.d: In this course, students examine the strategies required of meeting and event planners tasked with the development and coordination of food and beverage functions within a variety of meetings and events. Students interpret food and beverage consumption patterns of meeting attendees, identify various service requirements, meal styles and functions, distinguish between on and off-site catering requirements, examine the relationship between the catering department and other departments within a hotel, plan and design sample group menus, and determine appropriate pricing strategies and contractual requirements for meeting and event group functions.

r: This course has students examine event objectives and nonprofit sponsorship opportunities against the event budget, apply industry software to manage attendee registration, volunteer management, audiovisual requirements, and event-space allocation, and produce reports on the key service providers tied to accommodations, transportation, ancillary activities, and post-event evaluations. The heavy reliance on software for registration, tracking, and reporting maps directly to O*NET computer-interaction and information-processing activities, which observed-usage data identifies as the largest category of current AI use, spanning both consumer and enterprise API traffic. The course carries no accreditation lock, and its corequisite relationship to EVT 4100 is only moderately protective under the deterministic rule. At 24 months, the instrumental need to learn today's specific software workflows is already partially eroded by AI-assisted reporting and data management, but full deployment across hospitality operations remains uneven: Medium.

By 2031, AI-integrated event-management platforms will plausibly automate registration tracking, volunteer scheduling, AV-requirement compilation, and post-event evaluation reporting with limited manual input, consistent with evidence that computer-interaction and data-processing tasks form the largest and fastest-growing category of observed AI usage across both consumer and enterprise settings. The course's core competence — operating software to manage attendee, volunteer, and vendor data and generate structured service-provider reports — is precisely the kind of processing-and-documentation work these systems already perform competently. No accreditation requirement or strong foundational role caps the erosion at this horizon; the corequisite link to EVT 4100 does not meet the threshold for a long-horizon cap. The instrumental case for a student to manually operate these systems, rather than supervise an AI-driven version, is substantially weakened: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI-native event platforms handling registration, volunteer coordination, AV logistics compilation, and post-event reporting largely autonomously, and the software-operation rationale for this course is largely eroded. No institutional lock-in applies in this hospitality program, so nothing caps the rating at the ten-year horizon. The honest uncertainty is how much human oversight event operations still require when the underlying systems make consequential allocation decisions — sponsorship matching, event-space assignment — errors in which could carry real cost, though the course description frames the work as operational and reporting rather than adversarial or high-stakes judgment. The rating holds at High, reflecting that the specific, software-mediated data-management tasks this course teaches sit squarely within AI's demonstrated processing and documentation strengths.
EVT 3010.d: In this course, students will examine event objectives and potential sponsorship opportunities for nonprofit events as they relate to the event budget. The course will provide students with an opportunity to apply current industry software to manage attendee registration, volunteer management, audiovisual requirements, and event space management. In addition, students will produce reports of the key service providers related to attendee accommodations, transportation, ancillary activities, and post-event evaluations.

r: Students coordinate and manage a hypothetical corporate meeting from start to finish, use industry-standard forms and meeting-management software, set goals and objectives, organize logistics, evaluate return on investment, analyze contractual needs, and assess risk with contingency planning. This is business-planning and analytical work — O*NET planning, analysis, and compliance-evaluation activities — closely resembling the office and management tasks that observed-usage data shows as a substantial and growing share of AI use. The course has no accreditation lock and does not scaffold later required courses in this catalog, leaving task automatability the main driver of the rating. At 24 months, meeting planning software already assists much of this work, but full end-to-end automation of goal-setting and ROI evaluation is not yet the norm: Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft meeting goals and objectives, logistics plans, ROI evaluations, and risk-contingency documents for a described corporate meeting with limited human direction, consistent with productivity research showing large gains on professional writing and business-analysis tasks, and with observed-usage data showing office and planning tasks as a prominent and growing share of real AI use. Because the course's deliverables are template-like planning and evaluation documents rather than embodied on-site management, and because no accreditation or foundational-scaffolding factor applies, the base rate computed from rising task automatability governs the rating without a cap. The instrumental case for a student to personally build these plans and evaluations, rather than direct and verify an AI-generated version, is substantially weakened: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems handling most corporate meeting planning end to end — objective-setting, logistics organization, ROI modeling, contractual-needs and risk analysis — and the manual-planning rationale for this course is largely superseded. No institutional lock-in exists for meeting-management instruction in this hospitality program, so nothing caps the rating at the ten-year horizon. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the negotiation and stakeholder-management residue — vendor bargaining, resolving on-site conflicts during the meeting itself — remains distinctly valuable human work as the planning layer automates, a residue this course description touches only lightly relative to its planning and evaluation content. The rating holds at High, hedged by that negotiation residue but anchored by the largely automatable planning core.
EVT 3100.d: This course focuses on how to coordinate and manage corporate meetings. Students organize a hypothetical corporate meeting from beginning to end. Hospitality industry standard forms and meeting management software are introduced and utilized. Students also develop goals and objectives, organize logistical components, and evaluate the return on investment of the meeting. Students also analyze contractual needs based on goals and objectives of the meeting. Potential risks to the meeting are assessed and considerations for a corresponding contingency plan are outlined.

r: This course focuses on program planning and logistics management for citywide conventions with corresponding trade shows, plus freestanding tradeshow and exhibition management, culminating in a project presentation demonstrating the student's ability to schedule, promote, budget, and execute a large-scale, multi-day, multi-venue meeting with an exhibition. The planning, scheduling, and budgeting components map to O*NET organizing and coordinating activities that observed-usage data shows are already common AI applications, particularly for drafting schedules and promotional materials, but 'execute' signals a real on-site, multi-venue coordination component that keeps embodiment from being purely digital. No accreditation lock applies, and the course does not scaffold other required coursework in this catalog. At 24 months the planning artifacts are increasingly AI-assisted, while live, multi-venue execution judgment remains largely human: Medium.

By 2031, AI planning tools will plausibly generate scheduling, promotional, and budget plans for large multi-venue conventions and trade shows with considerable fluency, consistent with evidence on strong productivity gains for structured planning and writing tasks and on rising diffusion of such tools into meeting-industry operations. The on-site execution component — coordinating a live, multi-day, multi-venue exhibition — provides some protection, but it is a smaller share of the graded coursework than the planning and budgeting artifacts the course description emphasizes, so that protection is not strong enough to trigger a dampener under the deterministic rule. No accreditation lock or foundational role caps the erosion at this horizon. The instrumental case for personally producing these planning documents, rather than directing and verifying an AI-generated version, weakens substantially: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI handling most of the scheduling, promotional, and budgeting work for large conventions and trade shows, and the planning-document rationale for this course is largely superseded. No institutional lock-in exists in this hospitality program to cap the rating at the ten-year horizon. The honest uncertainty concerns how much live, multi-venue exhibition coordination — resolving real-time conflicts across vendors, space, and schedules during the event itself, once automated planning has set the baseline — remains a distinctly human competence as the upstream planning automates; that residue is real but was not weighted heavily enough in the course's own emphasis on the planning-and-presentation artifact to change the deterministic outcome. The rating holds at High, hedged by that on-site coordination residue.
EVT 3200.d: Students in this course focus upon program planning and logistics management for citywide conventions with corresponding trade shows, as well as freestanding tradeshow and exhibition management. Student outcomes include a project presentation demonstrating the student's ability to schedule, promote, budget, and execute a large-scale, multi-day and/or multi-venue meeting with an exhibition.

r: Students learn to recognize business situations requiring bargaining or negotiation, identify and analyze the letters of agreement and contracts common across hotels, convention centers, restaurants, special-event centers, country clubs, and indoor and outdoor festival space, and create and appraise banquet and event orders, entertainment riders, and agreements among clients, facilities, and third-party planning companies or consultants. Contract analysis and drafting is document-centric work that maps to O*NET interpreting and documenting activities, a category where professional-writing research shows large time savings and quality gains from AI assistance. Live bargaining retains an interpersonal, real-time element that offers some protection, and no accreditation lock applies to this hospitality elective. At 24 months, contract drafting is increasingly AI-assisted while the negotiation itself remains a human skill: Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft, redline, and appraise banquet and event orders, entertainment riders, and multi-party facility agreements with high fluency, consistent with evidence of large productivity and quality gains for professional document writing and with growing observed use of AI for contract-style office tasks. The negotiation component — real-time bargaining to reach acceptable terms for both parties — is embodied and interpersonal enough to offer some protection, but it represents a narrower share of the course's graded content than contract creation and analysis, so it does not trigger the dampener under the deterministic rule. No accreditation or foundational-scaffolding factor caps the erosion at this horizon. The instrumental case for personally drafting and appraising these documents, rather than directing and verifying an AI-generated version, weakens substantially: High.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems competently drafting and appraising the full range of event-industry contracts and letters of agreement across hotel, convention-center, restaurant, and festival-space contexts, and the document-production rationale for this course is largely superseded. No institutional lock-in exists in this hospitality program to cap the rating at the ten-year horizon. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much real-time bargaining judgment remains distinctly human as contract generation automates, and how much a mis-negotiated or poorly-vetted AI-drafted agreement's error cost pushes verification demands back toward requiring trained human review — a jagged-frontier dynamic this rating cannot resolve confidently at the ten-year horizon. The rating holds at High, anchored by the largely automatable contract-document core and hedged by the negotiation and verification residue.
EVT 4020.d: In this course, students explore a variety of event and meeting industry negotiations and contracts. Students develop the necessary skills to recognize business situations requiring bargaining and/or negotiation to achieve acceptable outcomes for both parties. The course emphasizes the importance of being able to identify and analyze the numerous and varied letters of agreement and contracts prevalent in the meeting and event industry, including but not limited to hotel, convention center, restaurant, special event center, country club and both indoor and outdoor festival space. Students create and appraise banquet and event orders (BEOs), entertainment riders, and agreements between clients facilities and third-party, independent planning companies or consultants.

r: Building on prior events coursework, this course develops leadership skills in crisis planning and management, drawing on Auraria Campus and industry expertise to equip students to prepare for and reduce the likelihood and impact of public health emergencies, natural disasters, infrastructure failures, major technology breaches, and terrorist attacks, and to lead disaster-recovery efforts when needed. This maps to O*NET decision-making, team-development, and monitoring activities in a genuinely high-stakes, adversarial domain where task-exposure research finds critical-thinking-intensive work least exposed. Verification burden is severe: a flawed crisis plan or a mishandled real emergency carries safety consequences with non-obvious failure modes, which drops the rating one band under the deterministic rule. No accreditation lock applies, but the leadership and real-time crisis-response core keeps the instrumental case intact at 24 months: Low.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft crisis-plan templates, compile risk checklists, and model scenario impacts across the five named hazard categories with real fluency, consistent with capability trends showing rapid growth in structured document generation and reasoning over multi-step scenarios. But leading an organization's actual response to a public-health emergency, infrastructure failure, or attack requires real-time judgment under pressure and interpersonal team leadership that task-exposure research does not classify as automatable, and the verification burden remains severe — an AI-generated contingency plan that fails during an actual crisis has costly, non-obvious consequences. That verification dampener holds the rating one band below its capability-driven base. The instrumental case is only partially eroded: Medium, reflecting that planning documentation increasingly automates while crisis leadership does not.

A decade out, AI crisis-planning and scenario-modeling tools will be considerably more capable, and much of the documentation, checklist-generation, and preliminary risk-modeling work underlying contingency planning across the five named hazard categories could be substantially automated. But leading people through an actual public-health emergency, natural disaster, infrastructure failure, technology breach, or attack remains an embodied, high-stakes, real-time leadership task where a wrong call has severe and not-immediately-visible consequences, keeping the verification-burden dampener in force under the deterministic rule even at this horizon. No accreditation mandate protects the course, so the cap comes entirely from the severity of getting crisis response wrong. The rating holds at Medium, with genuine uncertainty about how much scenario planning automates around a still-human crisis-leadership core by 2036.
EVT 4030.d: Drawing upon knowledge and skills acquired in pre- requisite events courses, this course will allow students to gain relevant leadership skills in areas of crisis planning and management. This course will provide students from across the Auraria Campus as well as industry leaders the skills and tools to lead efforts to prepare for crises within their organizations as well as implement preventions that will reduce the likelihood and impact of 5 different kinds of crisis (i.e., public health emergencies, natural disasters, infrastructure failures, major technology breaches, and terrorist attacks) while enabling disaster recovery when necessary.

r: This capstone course has students determine the required equipment, professional personnel, and licensing needed to construct a special event — with specific emphasis on outdoor festivals, social galas, and fundraisers — appraise vendors and expert support staff for logistical and technical production challenges, and propose communication techniques for working with stakeholder groups. Unlike the planning-heavy EVT courses, the applied work here is centered on physically constructing and running a live event: equipment, on-site personnel, and technical production problems. These map to O*NET physical-execution and equipment-inspection activities that task-exposure research consistently places among the least automatable categories. No accreditation lock applies, but embodiment does the protective work. At 24 months the instrumental need to learn hands-on event production is essentially unaffected: Low.

By 2031, AI tools will more capably assist with vendor sourcing, equipment specification, and logistics documentation feeding into event production, but the graded core of this course — appraising and coordinating equipment, personnel, and expert support staff to resolve live technical and logistical production challenges on site — is embodied, physical, real-time work that a language or planning model does not perform on the student's behalf. GDPval-style evidence on real occupational deliverables shows current models still fall short of full human parity even on largely digital tasks, reinforcing that physical production judgment lags further behind. No institutional lock-in applies, so protection here comes entirely from embodiment. The instrumental case for personally learning to construct and run a special event remains largely intact: Low.

A decade out, event-logistics software and AI-assisted vendor management will be considerably more capable, and the administrative shell around event production — contracts, schedules, vendor lists — will likely automate further. But the specific competence this capstone course builds is the physical, hands-on construction and on-site technical troubleshooting of a live festival, gala, or fundraiser, which sits squarely in the manual and physical-execution categories task-exposure research treats as low-exposure even under aggressive capability growth. No accreditation mandate protects the course, but embodiment alone is sufficient under the deterministic rule to hold the rating down. The wide uncertainty band concerns how much planning and vendor-coordination work migrates to AI tools around this still-physical production core, not whether hands-on production skill remains instrumentally necessary. Rating holds Low.
EVT 4100.d: In this course, students examine the required equipment, professional personnel and licensing required to construct a special event, with specific emphasis placed on outdoor festivals, social galas, and fundraisers. Students appraise the appropriate vendors and expert support staff required to resolve specific logistical and/or technical production challenges. Students further examine the needs of event stakeholders and propose communication techniques appropriate for working with each group effectively.

r: EVT 4200 asks students to compare United States and international meeting practices across venues, business norms, budgeting, currency exposure, program planning, and risk management, then propose cross-cultural etiquette and protocol responses to logistics miscommunication. These tasks map onto Getting Information, Analyzing Data or Information, and Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards. Current models already draft comparative venue memos, currency-risk summaries, and etiquette guides competently, and Anthropic Economic Index data shows Computer and Mathematical work and writing-adjacent office tasks dominate present usage, consistent with this course's deliverables. Diffusion nonetheless lags capability: Census BTOS finds only a minority of firms using AI operationally through 2025, and cross-jurisdictional regulatory or currency assumptions still need a planner able to catch subtly wrong compliance claims. No licensure or accreditation clock-hour mandate applies. The binding constraint is planning-exposure rather than embodiment, since described tasks are comparative analysis, not on-site execution. Rated Medium: instrumentally useful, not yet substitutive.

By 2031 the comparative-analysis and budgeting work at the core of EVT 4200 is more plausibly automatable at the Realized Task Automatability level, since capability trends (METR/Epoch task-time-horizon doubling every four to seven months) suggest multi-step research and drafting across venues, currency conditions, and risk frameworks will be routinely competent. Task-exposure research classifies analytical, writing-heavy occupational activities as strongly and positively associated with exposure, and this course's deliverables (comparative memos, protocol documents, risk matrices) fit that profile closely. Verification burden remains real but moderate rather than severe: errors are costly but not adversarial or hidden, so a checked draft is plausible workflow. No institutional lock-in constrains the trajectory; the course carries no licensure or accreditation credit-hour floor. The planning-exposure binding constraint persists, with no embodiment protection since the coursework itself is analytical rather than on-site. Rated High, though adoption unevenness within hospitality firms could still slow realized displacement of this specific analytical skill set.

A ten-year view for EVT 4200 has to be hedged: capability projections (compute scaling roughly fivefold per year, per Epoch estimates) point toward AI systems handling comparative meeting-practice research, currency and budget modeling, and cross-cultural protocol drafting close to expert quality, but macro productivity work (Acemoglu) cautions that realized economy-wide displacement from such gains has historically stayed modest even under fast capability growth, and hospitality firm adoption could remain uneven relative to sectors like software. GDPval-style evidence suggests leading models approach but do not yet reach parity with human experts on realistic occupational deliverables, and international risk and compliance judgment carries error costs serious enough to keep a verification step in the loop. No licensure or credit-hour mandate offers structural protection, so the trajectory tracks capability and diffusion rather than institutional lock-in. The planning-exposure framing still governs, since no embodied execution appears in the course description. Rated High, with genuine uncertainty about pace.
EVT 4200.d: Students in this course compare and contrast domestic and global meeting and event planning theories and practice. The analysis includes the differences between the United States and international destinations with regard to venues, business practices, budgeting and currency issues, program planning, and risk management. Students examine potential areas of cross-cultural miscommunication and logistics management during the planning process and propose appropriate international etiquette and protocols.

r: EVT 4300 teaches Event Design Methodology: stakeholder alignment, pre- and post-event empathy mapping, the event canvas, event delta, and prototyping, applied to physical and visual mapping of venue spaces, attendee traffic flow, and interaction patterns. These activities map to Thinking Creatively, Developing Objectives and Strategies, Interacting With Computers, and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others. Task-exposure research finds strong positive association for writing- and framework-heavy tasks, and structured design-thinking artifacts like canvases and empathy maps are exactly the kind of templated documents current models draft well. But translating those drafts into a floor plan that actually serves real attendee flow through a physical space is a newer, less-validated use of generative design tools, so verification burden is elevated relative to EVT 4200's comparative-analysis work: subtly wrong spatial assumptions are non-obvious failures. No licensure constraint applies, and the course also underpins EVT 4200 as a prerequisite, giving it modest scaffolding weight. Rated Medium.

By 2031, EVT 4300's design-methodology deliverables — empathy maps, stakeholder alignment documents, event canvases, prototype iterations — remain instrumentally useful to teach even as drafting assistance improves, because the course's distinctive value is translating those artifacts into spatial judgments about how real attendees move through and experience a physical venue. Capability trends (METR/Epoch) suggest AI handles longer, multi-step creative-strategy tasks more competently by this horizon, and Anthropic Economic Index usage data shows writing and planning documents are already common AI use cases, so the templated-artifact half of this course is more exposed than the spatial-translation half. Verification burden stays moderate rather than low, since misjudged traffic flow or attendee experience is a non-obvious failure mode that only shows up once an event runs. No accreditation or licensure floor applies. As the prerequisite-scaffolding role documented at 24 months persists, this stays capped near, but does not clearly exceed, Medium; treated here as Medium given continued uncertainty about spatial-design maturity.

Over a ten-year horizon, generative spatial-design tools plausibly mature enough that the traffic-flow and attendee-interaction visualization work in EVT 4300 becomes more routinely AI-assisted alongside the already-exposed canvas and empathy-mapping artifacts, following the fast compute-scaling trend Epoch estimates at roughly fivefold per year. GDPval-style evidence shows leading models approaching, though still short of, human-expert parity on realistic design deliverables, which tempers a confident full-substitution claim. Jagged-frontier findings matter directly here: outside a model's genuine competence, users relying on AI design suggestions have shown meaningfully lower accuracy despite confidence, and physical-space judgment about real human comfort and movement is a plausible edge of that frontier. No licensure or accreditation mandate constrains the course, and its prerequisite role for EVT 4200 offers only modest, non-capping scaffolding protection. Given both improving generative-design capability and unresolved verification difficulty for spatial judgments, this horizon is rated High, with substantial uncertainty about whether spatial-design maturity actually arrives on this timeline.
EVT 4300.d: Students in this course use Event Design Methodology to create both physical and visual mapping. Course activities focus upon analyzing the critical conditions and situations necessary to plan and build engaging event experiences. Students use design technology to visualize spaces, traffic flow, and meeting attendee interactions. By employing a visual representation prior to a meeting, the student event planners can create events that assure attendees have transformative experiences during their event or meeting where stakeholder the viewpoint is visualized so planners may better understand attendee needs. The design methodology utilizes tools such as, stakeholder alignment, pre, and post-event empathy mapping, event canvas, event delta, and the event prototype. Exercise and Sport Sciences
